p: Muhammad Dara Shikoh was born at Ajmer on 20 March 1615, the first son and third child of Prince Khurram, the later Shah Jahan, and Mumtaz Mahal. He studied the Quran, history, Persian poetry and calligraphy, and beside his native Persian learned Hindi, Arabic and later Sanskrit. He and his elder sister Jahanara Begum were their father's favourite children.

On 1 February 1633 he married his half-cousin Nadira Banu Begum at Agra, and he contracted no other marriage. In the same year he was appointed heir apparent, which Shah Jahan formally confirmed on 10 September 1642 with the title Shahzada-e-Buland Iqbal, Prince of High Fortune. He was made governor of Allahabad in 1645 and of Gujarat in 1648.

Dara followed the Qadiri Sufi saint Mian Mir of Lahore, to whom Mullah Shah Badakhshi introduced him, and the mystic Sarmad Kashani, and he formed a friendship with the seventh Sikh Guru, Guru Har Rai. The treatise known as Majma-ul-Bahrain was written in Persian in 1654–55. His Persian version of fifty Upanishads, completed in 1657 and often called Sirr-i-Akbar, proposes in its introduction that the hidden book named in the Quran is the Upanishads. Annemarie Schimmel notes that he remained committed to the fundamentals of Islam and repeatedly called himself a Hanafi Qadiri.

He was a patron of painting, music and dancing, tastes that Aurangzeb frowned upon. The album of paintings and calligraphy that bears his name was presented to his wife in 1641–42; after her death the inscriptions linking it to him were deliberately erased.

After Samugarh he retreated by Delhi, Lahore, Multan and Thatta to Kathiawar, where Shah Nawaz Khan, governor of Gujarat, helped him raise a new army. After the rout at Deorai on 11 March 1659 he sought refuge in Sindh with the Afghan chieftain Malik Jeevan, whose life he had saved more than once, but Malik Jeevan seized him and informed Aurangzeb, whose army took him on 10 June 1659.

In Delhi he was paraded through the streets in chains on an elephant. A convocation of nobles and clergy called by Aurangzeb declared him a threat to the public peace and an apostate from Islam, and he was killed in front of his son on the night of 30 August 1659. He was buried in an unidentified grave in Humayun's tomb. In 2020 Sanjeev Kumar Singh, a municipal engineer, identified one of three unmarked cenotaphs beneath the dome as his, relying on the Alamgirnama; several historians and archaeologists have accepted the identification.

notes: Death date: the article gives 30 August 1659 with '9 September Gregorian' in brackets; I used 30 August as in the lede.
The article names both Dharmat and Samugarh as Dara's battles with Aurangzeb; the existing entry already has Samugarh and Deorai, so the war itself is not retold.
Manucci's account of the severed head sent to Shah Jahan is left out (one traveller's account, and length).
The article dates the Yoga Vasistha commission '1006 A.H.', which cannot be right for Dara (born 1615); left out.
The article says the Delhi library was 'originally built in 1637'; left out as unclear.
